sections.html:
Jefferson houses the two offices you need. Values and value disputes are the auditor's, at the courthouse, 25 W Jefferson St, 440-576-3783. Billing and collecting are the treasurer's. Direct questions about a bill, a payoff for a sale, or a delinquent balance to the treasurer.

Ashtabula County fills Ohio's northeastern corner, with Jefferson as seat. In 2020 it had 97,574 residents and 46,237 housing units, 14.9% of them vacant. Owners lived in 71.0% of occupied homes.

The county covers 1,368 square miles, 49% of it Lake Erie water. Three cities (Ashtabula, Conneaut and Geneva) sit beside seven villages: Andover, Geneva-on-the-Lake, Jefferson, North Kingsville, Orwell, Roaming Shores and Rock Creek. Lake-effect snow falls often, so roofs, gutters and drainage matter to buyers.

A lakeside village house and an inland farmhouse can fall in quite different taxing districts. Keep the parcel number from your bill handy, since every question below starts there.

sections.h2: How to challenge your property value
sections.html:
The county's complaint season runs January 1 through March 31, with filings handed to the auditor for the Board of Revision. ORC 5715.19(A)(1) in fact stretches the deadline to March 31 of the following year or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later. Mail counts as filed on its postal postmark date, not a private meter date.

The Board changes values, never tax dollars, and you carry the burden of proof. Gather paperwork:

  • A closing statement and contract from a recent purchase.
  • An independent appraisal.
  • Contractor quotes for defects.
  • Rent rolls and expense records for a rental.

Two arguments get nowhere: how quickly your tax rose, and how a neighbor's parcel is valued. Deliver paper forms to the auditor, or e-file to bor@ashtabulacounty.gov. Call the Board at 440-576-1484 on weekdays between eight and half past four.

A certified letter announcing the hearing should arrive at least ten days early. The Board owes you a ruling within 180 days after the last day to file. An owner who disagrees has 30 days from the decision letter's postmark to appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals in Columbus or the Court of Common Pleas in Jefferson. File the notice of appeal with the Board of Revision as well as the forum you pick.

Two more rules from ORC 5715.19 affect timing:

  • Pending a decision, you may pay on your claimed value, and the treasurer must take it.
  • Should the final value exceed your claim, interest runs on the gap from the original due date.
  • Give the Board everything. Evidence withheld there may be barred on appeal.

Not right away. After a complaint on a parcel, subsection (A)(2) blocks further complaints for the remainder of that interim period, unless something changed after the lien date. Qualifying changes are an arm's-length sale, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement, or a drop of at least fifteen percent in occupancy that hurts the property economically.

A school board or other party may answer a large request with a counter-complaint, and the threshold is $17,500 in taxable value.

Begin with the auditor's parcel record: confirm year built and any additions, which buyers and lenders always ask about. Then call the treasurer for the current balance, remembering the second half if it is unpaid. Weigh a complaint before March 31. A lower value can ease a listing, and a pending case changes what you tender. Then set aside the transfer fee for closing and ask about a county transfer tax. Hand the title company all of it early so nothing surprises you at the table.

A good file is short and ties each paper to one claim. Lead with the strongest proof of market value, usually a recent closing statement or an independent appraisal. Add repair estimates if defects hold the value down, and rent and expense statements if the property earns income. Label each page, make a copy for the Board, and keep one for yourself. Since evidence you hold back can be shut out of a later appeal, put everything in at the first hearing rather than saving some for round two.

Plan for the clock as well. The hearing notice comes by certified mail, and the Board has 180 days from the last filing day to rule, so a complaint filed in March may still be open when you want to list. Tell your agent and the title company, and keep paying on your claimed value so nothing falls behind.

Ohio rules that apply to an Ashtabula County sale
TopicRule
Complaint windowJanuary 1 through March 31
Appeal after decision30 days from the postmark on the letter
Hearing noticeCertified mail, ten days or more before the hearing
Standard payment datesFull bill by December 31, or half then and the rest by June 20
Deed transfer fee$1 minimum, or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, if higher

Those are the statewide baselines. The exact dates for your parcel are on your own bill or from the treasurer.

sections.h2: What the auditor charges on transfer
sections.html:
On a deed transfer the auditor collects the greater of $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value, with any fraction rounded up to a full $100 (ORC 319.54(G)(3)). Sellers pay. A Chapter 322 transfer tax, if the commissioners enacted one, is added, so check with the auditor.

The buyer files a value statement alongside. ORC 319.202 has that form record whether the seller had a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction or farm-use valuation, and farmland leaving the program can owe a recoupment charge. Spousal gifts, parent-to-child gifts and delinquent-tax sales are exempt.

Ask the treasurer for a payoff before you sign a sales contract. Unpaid taxes appear in the title search and normally come out of the seller's proceeds at closing. A pending value complaint should be mentioned to the title company, since the tender rule above may set the amount due.

Empty houses, roofs battered by lake-effect winters and parcels with back taxes can all sell as-is using the same payoff steps. Get the parcel record from the auditor first so acreage and building details agree with your deed.

A cash buyer leaves the sequence intact. The payoff, transfer fee and value statement still come first. What disappears is the lender's appraisal and underwriting, so timing depends mostly on how quickly the treasurer and auditor respond.

faqs.q: When can I file a property value complaint in Ashtabula County?
faqs.a: The county's window is January 1 through March 31, though the statute allows a later cutoff when first-half collection closes after March 31. Mail is dated by postmark.

faqs.q: Which office answers questions about an Ashtabula County tax bill?
faqs.a: The treasurer answers for bills and payments. For values and exemptions, the auditor is at 440-576-3783, and the Board of Revision line is 440-576-1484.

faqs.q: Does the Board of Revision lower my tax bill?
faqs.a: Only indirectly. It changes the value, and the tax follows. Tax increases and neighbors' values are not arguments it will weigh.

faqs.q: Can I appeal a Board of Revision decision?
faqs.a: Yes. You have 30 days from the postmark on the decision letter to go to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals in Columbus or the Court of Common Pleas in Jefferson. Copy the Board of Revision on the notice.

faqs.q: How much is the auditor's transfer charge?
faqs.a: The greater of $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction. The seller pays, plus any county transfer tax the auditor can confirm.
